title: Sakya
hook: the school of the gray earth, led by the Khon family

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three-year retreat: a long stretch of practice behind a closed door, kept by Kagyu and other schools. Did you pick one practice to keep every day this month? A new week starts now. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

A hillside in southern Tibet, and the soil on it is pale. Not brown, not red: a dusty, ashy gray, the color of a cooled fire. Tradition says a man of the Khon family built a monastery on that slope, and the place took its name from the ground under it. Sakya. The gray earth. A whole school of Tibetan Buddhism is named for a patch of dirt, and for a long time it was led by one family, parents and children and nephews, handing the work down at home as much as from the teaching throne. Today, another of the great Tibetan schools, and the oddly homely way it began.
screen: `A HILLSIDE OF PALE SOIL.` → `THE KHON FAMILY BUILDS THERE.` → `A SCHOOL NAMED FOR THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Sakya is usually translated as gray earth, or pale earth, after that hillside. Plenty of schools carry a founder's name or an idea. This one is named for a place you could kneel down and touch. That's worth holding onto: in this school the teaching has an address. Second, the family. The Sakya tradition remembers the Khon family as its holders. Leadership passed down within that family, often from uncle to nephew, and the head of the school came to be called the Sakya Trizin, the holder of the Sakya throne. In some traditions authority moves by election or by finding a reborn teacher. In this one, for much of its story, it moved through a household. Third, the scholar. Out of that family came Sakya Pandita, remembered as a great learned man. He wrote on logic and on how to read the teachings carefully, and he wrote short verses of good advice about speaking, giving and choosing friends, short enough to remember. His nephew Phagpa traveled to the court of the Mongol rulers, and tradition says he devised a written script for them. A family from a gray hillside ended up teaching at the edge of an empire. Fourth, what a family carries. A lineage is usually pictured as a line of teachers. Sakya adds something warmer and messier: kitchens, inheritances, a young person who grows up knowing the teaching is the family business and has to decide whether to take it on. The gray earth is not only a place. It is a reminder that the teaching came down through ordinary people, who had to agree to carry it.
screen: `GRAY EARTH: A SCHOOL WITH AN ADDRESS.` · `THE KHON FAMILY HOLDS THE THRONE.` · `SAKYA PANDITA AND HIS NEPHEW PHAGPA.` · `A LINEAGE THAT IS ALSO A HOUSEHOLD.` · then, large: `THE GRAY EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one family's story. It can be your own, or a friend's, or someone you've only heard about. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing that was handed down in that family: a recipe, a trade, a phrase, a way of praying, a stubbornness. Ask yourself, quietly, who first carried it, and who chose to keep carrying it. You don't need answers. Just let the question rest for a moment, the way the gray earth rests under the monastery. The bell holds the time.
Sakya. The gray earth: a Tibetan school named for a pale hillside, long held by the Khon family. Today's word.

Your line: the gray earth. Today, notice the ground under one place that matters to you, a kitchen floor, a doorstep, a path. Somebody made that a place where things get handed down. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Sakya Buddhists study and practice in monasteries and centers of the Sakya school, honoring the Sakya Trizin as the head of the tradition and the Khon family as its historic holders.
